title: Why Rejoin UNIDO? A Conversation with Its Leaders
label: 15 Sep 2026 · UNIDO evidence
summary: The International Agreements Committee questioned three senior UNIDO officials about why the UK should formally rejoin the UN industrial development agency. The witnesses described reforms that tripled funding and doubled project delivery, gave examples of UK-funded work on steel and cement decarbonisation, rice farming in Ghana, and green recovery in Ukraine, and argued that membership would give the UK a vote and oversight over an organisation it already funds heavily. Committee members pressed on whether the same results could be achieved by simply funding projects bilaterally, and whether reforms would outlast the current leader.

chapters.title: What changed after the UK left?
chapters.takeaway: UNIDO says it has gotten much better at managing money and delivering projects since the UK quit, and that its core mission was never really the problem.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome, everyone. Today we're looking at UNIDO, the UN's industrial development agency, and why the UK might rejoin it. We have three senior people from UNIDO here to explain.

turns.speaker: Lord German
turns.text: This is a 'what's changed?' question. When the UK left, there were real worries about how well UNIDO was run. What have you actually done since then to fix those problems?

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: That's the right question. I joined around the time the UK left, so I've seen it first-hand. The UK's complaints back then were fair and very clearly explained: the issue was never what we do, it was how efficiently we did it.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: About four years ago a new boss took over, a former German government minister who was actually quite sceptical of the UN and ran things like a businessperson. He did two big shake-ups of our headquarters.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: We looked hard at all our back-office work — finance, buying supplies, hiring — with outside business advisers, and cut out a whole layer of management. We didn't fire anyone; we just didn't replace people who retired.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: The results are striking. In four years we've tripled the money we bring in from partners, including the UK. The UK is now our second-biggest donor. And we've doubled the amount of actual project work we deliver, to about £400 million this year.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: One big change is that we've opened up to private business. We're not just charity; we can help UK companies get a foot in markets in Africa, Latin America and Asia that they couldn't easily reach before.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: Even the UK gave us a test project — we started with a few million pounds and it grew to about £140 million because it worked well. That shows the reforms are real.

chapters.title: Why is rural energy still so hard?
chapters.takeaway: Energy investment is still concentrated in a few countries, and one committee member says UNIDO needs to focus more on small local businesses that can't get any power.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: I travel to developing countries a lot, and I just came back from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Huge areas still have no electricity at all. You say you've reformed, but where is the money actually going, and how are you measuring whether it helps local businesses? I don't see it on the ground.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: That's a fair frustration. Most energy investment goes to a handful of countries. The poorest countries and small islands are still badly short of money. We host global meetings to push for more finance, and we help countries draw up plans to attract investment.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: But our special angle is that energy is the backbone, and industry is the engine that turns it into development. We're working with West African countries, for example, to process their minerals instead of just exporting raw materials.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: The problem is that most of these countries depend on very small businesses, and they can't grow without any power. Sometimes you need to start with the small local businesses and work up, not focus on the big picture first.

chapters.title: Reforming the whole UN family
chapters.takeaway: UNIDO says it's already ahead of a UN-wide reform push, and is now looking at sharing back-office work with other agencies that do it better.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: All UN agencies are under huge financial pressure right now. What is UNIDO doing as part of the Secretary-General's effort to shrink the UN's staff and programmes?

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: That effort is called UN80. Because of the UK's decision in 2012 and others, we'd already done a lot of this work before the current squeeze. So we were somewhat prepared.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: Our main job in the reform talks has been to be honest about who does what best. There's a lot of overlap between UN agencies. We've been mapping out which agency has the real advantage in each area, so we don't all duplicate each other.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: We're also asking whether we need our own HR and procurement departments when other agencies might do that faster and cheaper. We have the engineers and economists, but we don't have to be the best at payroll.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: Here's a concrete example. We've partnered with the UN's space agency, UNOOSA. We call it Space4Industry. We use satellite data and AI to help protect industrial zones from climate risks and to improve early warning systems.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: It's a good example of two agencies complementing each other instead of duplicating work.

chapters.title: What UK money actually does
chapters.takeaway: UK-funded projects include global standards for greener steel and cement, a Brazil-UK innovation link, and a facility that helped Namibia start producing hydrogen.

turns.speaker: Lord Stevenson of Balmacara
turns.text: You mentioned you get money from the UK. Can you give us two or three concrete examples of what that money has actually done on the ground?

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: Yes. First, we're working with the UK on global standards for counting carbon in steel and cement. That matters because those standards will shape global trade.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: Second, we're linking UK universities and small companies with Brazil to help it plan a greener steel and cement industry.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: Third, through a facility called Accelerate-to-Demonstrate, we've helped Namibia start its first hydrogen production programme. We've also helped with biogas from tea waste in Kenya. These bring UK technology and know-how to developing countries.

chapters.title: Can you scale up?
chapters.takeaway: Committee members say the world needs proof that projects can grow from small pilots to large-scale change, and ask whether UNIDO can deliver that.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: For decades, UK taxpayers have funded food security and farming projects. Can you give a practical example of how UNIDO, perhaps with the Food and Agriculture Organization, has helped small farmers, especially in Africa? If not now, please write to us.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: I can give one from Ghana. About half of West Africa's rice is imported, and around 20% of what's grown locally is lost after harvest. We developed a tool that farmers can hold in their hand to scan rice and track where losses happen.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: In six months we've cut losses from 20% to 13%. That project was funded by Japan, not the UK, but it shows what's possible and we want to copy it across West Africa.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: Can I suggest that agronomists — people who really know the soil — are the greatest asset any community has? Your technology is helpful, but you should make sure they're part of the mix too.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I believe private enterprise solves most of these problems, not the state. We already have a huge development office spending billions. What can you do that we can't do ourselves? That's the question we'll be asked.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: We have a network that others don't. Japan is giving us £200 million for Ukraine's recovery, for example. They know we have contacts with local governments, mayors, and experts on the ground that they can't reach alone.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: Italy gives us a lot too, partly because Italian coffee companies like Illy and Lavazza want independent proof that their supply chains are sustainable. We can provide that kind of trusted certification.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But we already work through you. Why do we need to formally join? It sounds like we have a good arrangement as it is.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: Because right now you're one of our biggest funders but you don't have a vote. If you join, you get a seat on our governing boards and a say over how the money is spent. It's about accountability.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: The membership fee is tiny compared to what you already give voluntarily. It's almost a no-brainer to become a member and hold us to account from the inside.

chapters.title: Why not just fund projects directly?
chapters.takeaway: Some members remain sceptical that membership adds value beyond simply funding good projects, and witnesses argue that being inside gives the UK influence and oversight.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: I've heard your reforms, but I'm not convinced joining is worth it. Why not just fund specific projects we care about and see the results, rather than join what could be a talking shop?

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: I spent years in the field in places like Chad and Madagascar. We built solar mini-grids, small hydropower systems, and trained former fighters for jobs. The work is very tangible — you can see the jobs and the change.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: The difference now is scale. A typical project used to be £2 million; now it can be £200 million because the private sector is involved. That's a completely different level of impact.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: Take Ukraine. We're running a large green recovery programme funded by Japan. The UK's Foreign Office came to us because we have people on the ground in western Ukraine that they didn't. We can connect their work with Japan's and make it go further.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: But doesn't that prove you'd be better off just funding a project we both care about and seeing the results?

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: No, because there's a next step. When a project ends, we need to bring in private investors to keep it going. That's why we set up a finance coalition at London Climate Action Week — to leverage private money for scale.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: The failure globally has been not scaling up. Everyone can point to good small projects. We need proof that agencies like yours can make things big. Otherwise we'll miss the Sustainable Development Goals.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury
turns.text: Can you convince the sceptics here what you mean by 'better to be inside'? That we're not just getting caught up in bureaucracy?

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Let me add another question. The current boss, Gerd Müller, sounds like he's done a great job. But what happens when he retires? Is this long-term? Please weave that in as you summarise.

chapters.title: The final pitch
chapters.takeaway: UNIDO argues that membership gives the UK influence over an organisation it already funds, and that reforms are being embedded beyond any one leader.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: It's about being part of the growth story. You have so much to offer — UK universities, consultancies, innovation. But other member states won't even let non-members bid for certain contracts.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: We want the UK involved in our next reforms — better IT, better results tracking, better governance. You can't do that from outside. What comes after our current boss? I can't promise, but the trend is strong and being a member helps ensure it continues.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: I've been at UNIDO longer than these two. I've seen the change under this Director-General. He's building a foundation that goes beyond his own term. We're embedding new ways of working with the private sector and new financial tools.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: On energy, the reason things don't scale is that rural demand is low. Industries provide the anchor load that makes a business case. We're helping countries prepare for bigger private and concessional finance.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: We're also training leaders inside the organisation so the reforms outlast any one person. There's a lot of enthusiasm to keep flying this flag.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you very much. That's been hugely helpful, and we appreciate your journey from Vienna. Safe travels home.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury
turns.text: Please keep supporting Lavazza.
